summary: A list of well-known socket numbers that Jon Postel assigned for public functions on the early ARPANET, with a general scheme for ranges such as network-wide standard functions and experimental ones. Sockets here were the addressing scheme of the old network control program, before ports. It was replaced by RFC 503.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists socket numbers for services on the early ARPANET. It also shows which services were listed at particular hosts, so users could look up where a function was available.

subtitle: A record of service numbers assigned to public functions on the early network.

tldr.problem: Network users and host operators needed a shared list of socket numbers for public network functions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns ranges to standard, host-specific, reserved, and experimental functions, names particular services, and lists services reported at individual hosts.
tldr.outcome: The list helped users find services and highlighted conflicts between assignments. RFC 503 replaced it.

today: RFC 433 was replaced by RFC 503. This document preserves an earlier set of assignments and reports of services on individual hosts.

sections.title: How a Socket Number Is Divided
sections.content: The RFC describes a socket number as a 40-bit quantity. Its first 8 bits specify the host, the next 24 bits are site-specific, and the final 8 bits are the AEN, or Another Eightbit Number. In these assignments, the host field applies across hosts unless noted, and the 24-bit field is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket number combines a host identifier with a number for a particular function. This list sets the site-specific part to zero and gives the function number in the AEN field.

sections.title: Ranges and Named Functions
sections.content:
The general ranges are 0–63 for network-wide standard functions, 64–127 for host-specific functions, 128–239 reserved for future use, and 240–255 for experimental functions. Named assignments include Telnet at 1, File Transfer at 3, Remote Job Entry at 5, Echo at 7, Discard at 9, and Character Generator at 19.

The document also points to specifications for assigned functions. It notes that some hosts were already offering useful public services on numbers that conflicted with the scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The number range indicates whether a function is standard across the network, specific to one host, reserved, or experimental. The RFC also gives numbers to named services such as Telnet and File Transfer.

sections.title: Services Reported by Hosts
sections.content: A host-by-host list records socket numbers and the services reported at each site. The RFC presents the list as an aid to network users and invites corrections or missing entries, including information about services that were not considered official.
sections.plainLanguage: The host list shows which services had been reported at each computer. The authors invite readers to send corrections and additions.

sections.title: Status of This List
sections.content: The unit metadata records RFC 503 as the document that replaced RFC 433. The assignments and host listings here therefore describe the earlier list, not a current service directory.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an earlier version of the socket list. RFC 503 later replaced it.
